segments.title: Modern warships as cruisers by function
segments.summary: Many modern surface combatants perform the traditional peacetime cruising role, while destroyer and frigate labels describe their wartime functions.
segments.body: From Mikasa, the discussion turns to what modern warships are in form and function. The argument treats modern surface combatants as cruisers in the traditional sense because their normal peacetime work consists of cruising roles. Destroyer and frigate labels are presented as descriptions of wartime function rather than the whole of a ship's service. This approach separates what a vessel is called from the work it performs in peacetime and war. It also explains why older classification terms may remain useful when thinking about modern fleets.

evidence.note: He describes modern ships as cruisers in the traditional peacetime-role sense and contrasts that with destroyer and frigate labels.

segments.title: Uncrewed assets around crewed task-group centres
segments.summary: Future task groups are imagined with crewed warships at the centre and uncrewed vessels forming the outer elements of each group.
segments.body: The proposed force structure places crewed ships at the centre of task groups, with uncrewed assets operating around their outer edges. Several such groups and their flotillas could then combine into a larger task force. The crewed warship remains the organising centre rather than disappearing from the formation. This arrangement is presented as a continuation of the naval practice of grouping supporting vessels around a principal ship. The naming problem matters because calling every vessel an uncrewed asset says little about the wartime function it performs.

evidence.note: He outlines crewed ships at the centre of groups with uncrewed assets around their edges and argues their wartime function needs recognition.

segments.title: Why "sloop" fits flexible uncrewed vessels
segments.summary: Mikasa's historical setting prompts a proposal to call adaptable uncrewed vessels "sloops," reflecting their role in doing whatever larger ships require.
segments.body: The proposal borrows the historical term sloop for future uncrewed vessels. In the period invoked, a sloop was expected to go wherever it was needed and do whatever work larger ships required. Its defining feature was flexible employment rather than one narrow mission. That makes "sloop" a functional alternative to the generic label "uncrewed asset," especially when wartime roles need to be distinguished. The term is proposed as an analogy for fleet function rather than a claim about identical hulls or technology.

evidence.note: He defines the historical sloop as a flexible vessel that performed what larger ships required and applies that analogy to uncrewed assets.
